lines.text: The British property market is a national obsession — newspapers devote entire supplements to house prices, and dinner-party conversation often turns to mortgages and valuations. Property types in Britain reflect centuries of architectural history and social change. The most common dwelling is the terraced house — rows of identical homes sharing side walls, built during the Victorian and Edwardian eras to house industrial workers. Semi-detached houses ('semis') share one wall with a neighbour and typically have a front and back garden. Detached houses stand alone on their own plot and command a premium. Bungalows — single-storey homes popular with retirees — are increasingly rare as land values push developers toward multi-storey builds. Flats (apartments) range from purpose-built blocks to conversions carved from large Victorian houses. A maisonette is a flat spread across two floors with its own entrance from the street. Cottages — traditionally small rural homes with thick walls and low ceilings — are now highly sought-after for their charm. New-build estates feature modern, energy-efficient homes but are often criticised for small rooms and lack of character. The 'property ladder' — the progression from first flat to family home — remains a defining aspiration of British life, though rising prices have made the first rung increasingly difficult to reach.

lines.text: For your budget, you'd be looking at either a Victorian terrace or a 1930s semi. Both offer good space and character.

lines.text: What's the difference in terms of layout and maintenance?

lines.text: Terraces are typically narrower but deeper — long back gardens. Semis are wider with side access to the garden. Semis tend to have better natural light.

lines.text: In England and Wales, you either own the land outright (freehold) or lease it for a set term (leasehold — often 99 or 125 years). Flats are usually leasehold; houses are usually freehold. 'Lease extension' and 'ground rent' are terms every flat buyer must understand.

lines.text: After World War II, local councils built millions of homes for affordable rent — 'council houses'. Under Right to Buy (introduced 1980), tenants could purchase their council home at a discount. This reshaped British housing but reduced social housing stock dramatically.
